opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key insight is that the raw number of possible configurations is a bit of a red herring. Take Go: there are more possible board positions than atoms in the universe, so obviously you can't brute-force it. Protein folding is the same; Levinthal's paradox points out that a protein could never sample all its possible shapes, yet in nature it folds in milliseconds. That tells you something important: these spaces aren't random. They have structure.

Natural systems, and even many human-designed ones like games, aren't uniformly distributed across that enormous space. They sit on a much lower-dimensional manifold, shaped by physics, chemistry, evolution, or the rules of the game. Only a tiny fraction of configurations are realistic or relevant. What a neural network is very good at is learning a model of that underlying structure from data, essentially an intuition about which regions of the space are worth exploring.

Once you have that learned model, you don't need to search everything. In AlphaGo, the policy network narrows down the plausible moves and the value network evaluates positions, so the search can be very guided and efficient. You're doing a tiny, smart search instead of an exhaustive one. AlphaFold works in a similar spirit: it has learned the regularities of how proteins fold, so it can go almost directly to the answer.

So my conjecture is that any pattern that can be generated or found in nature can be efficiently discovered and modeled by a classical learning algorithm. That's partly because nature itself has been shaped by processes like evolution, which build structure on top of structure, and that structure is learnable. It's one of the reasons I'm so optimistic about using AI for scientific discovery. Many of the hardest problems in science look intractable on paper because of combinatorial explosion, but if there's an underlying structure, and I think there often is, then learning systems can find it.

r002.rationale: It cites natural protein folding and says AlphaFold learns folding regularities, but does not claim classical computers can solve folding by modeling the underlying physical process.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is one of the most fascinating things we've learned over the last decade or so. If you look at something like Go, there are more possible board positions than there are atoms in the universe, so brute force is clearly hopeless. You can't enumerate your way out. And yet AlphaGo managed it, and I think the reason comes down to the fact that these spaces, although astronomically large, are not random. They have structure.

The way I think about it is that almost all of those configurations are irrelevant. If you take a Go board and scatter stones randomly, you get a position that no competent player would ever reach, and the same is true for protein folding. Of all the shapes a chain of amino acids could theoretically adopt, nature only uses a tiny, highly constrained subset, because physics and evolution have carved out a manifold of plausible structures within that enormous space. So the real question isn't "how big is the search space," it's "how big is the space of configurations that actually matter," and that is often vastly smaller.

Neural networks turn out to be very good at learning that manifold. They're function approximators that pick up on regularities, patterns, correlations, and when you train them on enough examples, they build up something like intuition. In the AlphaGo case, the policy network learned to look at a position and immediately suggest a handful of promising moves, out of hundreds of possibilities, the same way a strong human player's eye is drawn to the right part of the board. That prunes the tree enormously before you do any explicit search at all.

And then the other half of it, which I think is crucial, is that you combine that learned intuition with some form of search or reasoning. Intuition alone is fallible, and search alone is intractable, but together they're incredibly powerful. The network narrows things down to the regions worth exploring, and the search verifies and refines within those regions. That's roughly how I think humans do it too, actually. Chess grandmasters don't calculate more than amateurs do, they calculate better, because their pattern recognition tells them where to look.

So my view is that whenever you have a problem with a huge combinatorial space but an underlying structure that can be learned, and ideally an efficient way to evaluate or simulate candidate solutions, it's a good candidate for this approach. That was really our thesis with AlphaFold, and I think there are many more problems in science that fit that description, in materials, in chemistry, in mathematics. The size of the space isn't what makes a problem hard. It's whether there's a learnable structure hiding within it.

r002.rationale: It describes protein folding as constrained by physics and evolution, but does not present it as evidence that classical computers could solve folding by modeling the underlying physical process.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key is that an enormous space of possibilities doesn’t necessarily mean you have to search all of it. There can be structure in that space, and a neural network can learn to exploit that structure.

Take Go. The number of possible positions is astronomical, but a strong player doesn’t consider every continuation equally. They recognise patterns, they have an intuition about which moves are promising, and that guides their search. A neural network can learn something analogous: a policy that suggests where to look, and a value function that estimates how good a position is.

So you’re combining that learned intuition with search. You spend your computation on a tiny, useful fraction of the possibilities.

Of course, that doesn’t make every combinatorial problem tractable. If there’s no structure to exploit, or the structure is very difficult to learn, you can still be stuck. But the problems we care about often have much more regularity than their raw number of configurations would suggest.

r001.rationale: The response says learned structure and intuition can guide search through only a fraction of possibilities, but it does not explain gradients guiding toward a correctly specified objective.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the key is that an enormous space of possible configurations doesn’t necessarily mean you have to search all of it. There may be structure in that space that you can learn and exploit.

Take chess or Go. The number of possible games is astronomical, but a strong player doesn’t consider every continuation. They have an intuition about which moves are promising and which positions are good. A neural network can learn something like that intuition, and then search can focus on the parts of the tree that matter.

And in physical systems, the possibilities aren’t all equally likely either. There are constraints, regularities, and patterns. If a network can discover those, a problem that looks hopeless from a brute-force perspective can become tractable.

Of course, that doesn’t mean neural networks make every combinatorial problem easy. The question is whether there’s enough learnable structure in the particular problem—and whether you’ve got the right data and architecture to capture it.
